title: Galaxy Cluster Abell 383
caption: Galaxy cluster Abell 383, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

story: This Hubble portrait shows Abell 383, a massive cluster of galaxies. NASA released it with a study of distant supernovae, exploding stars whose light was amplified by the gravity of foreground clusters on its way to us.

A cluster's gravity bends and brightens light from objects far behind it, much as a glass lens bends light, an effect first predicted by Albert Einstein. Astronomers use these natural lenses to find objects too faint to see otherwise. To trust the view they need the lens's "prescription", a map of how strongly it magnifies, and that depends on all of the cluster's matter, including the dark matter that supplies most of its gravity.

Two teams found three supernovae behind different clusters, and two and possibly all three appear to be Type Ia explosions. That type reaches a consistent peak brightness, so comparing the observed and expected brightness measures the magnification directly. Both teams found that the results fit models of the clusters' dark matter.

understand.summary: Combines visible light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with infrared light from Wide Field Camera 3. F435W, F475W, F606W and F625W are shown in blue, F775W, F814W and F850W in green, and F105W, F110W, F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Much of the data is infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the long exposures gather far more light than an eye could.

explore: The supernovae turned up in the CLASH survey, a Hubble census of dark matter in 25 galaxy clusters, and their explosions took place between 7 billion and 9 billion years ago. The astronomers estimate they would need about 20 supernovae spread behind one cluster to map its whole field and confirm a lens model.
